screens.title: Design Patterns for Clean Code
screens.subtitle: Reusable blueprints that make code easier to read, extend, and maintain.

narration.text: Design patterns are not recipes to copy-paste. They are reusable blueprints that capture proven ways to structure parts of your program so code remains clear and adaptable. In this chapter you will see why patterns matter: they reduce conditional clutter, separate responsibilities, and communicate design intent to other developers. For example, replacing tangled if-else branches for payment processing with interchangeable payment strategies makes it straightforward to add a new method without touching existing checkout logic. We will study three practical patterns — Strategy, Factory Method, and Decorator — and link each to the software principles they support, like the Single Responsibility and Open/Closed principles. You’ll also learn to spot when a pattern is useful versus when it becomes over-engineering. Throughout we use concise code examples in C#, Java, and Python so you can practice implementing patterns idiomatically. By the end of the lesson you’ll understand what each pattern solves, how it helps make code cleaner, and a simple checklist to decide whether to apply one. Consider: what recurring design problem in your last project might become clearer with a pattern?

keyIdea.title: Chapter Focus
keyIdea.text: Use Strategy, Factory Method, and Decorator to make code extensible, decoupled, and easier to maintain — but avoid over-engineering.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Design Patterns for Clean Code
Design Patterns for Clean Code
Reusable blueprints that promote separation of concerns, extensibility, and clear intent.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Patterns provide templates for solving recurring design problems. They capture structure and responsibilities so teams share a common vocabulary. When used thoughtfully they map directly to SOLID principles and keep classes focused and easy to extend.

We will examine three patterns with code examples and common mistakes, then practice an Observer implementation. Each lesson highlights the problem, the pattern’s structure, and a concrete example you can implement immediately.

In this lesson
Strategy
Encapsulate algorithms and swap them at runtime to avoid conditional logic.
Factory Method
Defer object creation to subclasses to reduce coupling and follow DIP.
Decorator
Add behavior dynamically without modifying original components.
Why patterns matter
Patterns let you express structural solutions succinctly. They reduce cognitive load when reading code because other developers recognize the pattern and its intent. They also guide you toward separation of concerns and safer extension points.
Example snapshot
Imagine a checkout system that supports credit card and PayPal. Without patterns you end up with spike methods and conditional logic. With Strategy you give each payment method its own class and an interface the checkout uses, so adding a new gateway is a single new class and registration step.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives map learning to practical ability. First, you will recall what a design pattern is and why it exists: a reusable solution template that solves a recurring design problem. Second, you'll explain how specific patterns improve maintainability and extensibility by modeling responsibilities and extension points. Third, you will identify which pattern naturally fits common problems, such as replacing conditional logic or decoupling object creation. Fourth, you'll implement common patterns — the Strategy, Factory Method, and Decorator — using concise, idiomatic code examples. Each objective is chosen to move you from recognition to implementation. You will practice spotting the problem first, choosing a pattern that addresses that problem, and then applying it in a focused code example. Throughout, we emphasize the link between patterns and SOLID principles so you can reason about the design trade-offs. Finally, you’ll also learn to avoid the common pitfall of applying patterns too early, which leads to unnecessary complexity. These skills make your code not just functional, but communicative and maintainable.

keyIdea.title: Core Goal
keyIdea.text: Move from recognizing patterns to applying them in a way that supports SOLID design and avoids over-engineering.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Judgment
screens.subtitle: Apply patterns responsibly and avoid over-engineering

narration.text: In this companion objectives slide we focus on judgment and practice. You will learn to map a pattern choice to SOLID principles so you can justify a refactor. For example, you’ll see why Strategy supports Open/Closed and Single Responsibility by keeping algorithm code out of the client. You will also practice communicating design intent — a well-applied pattern becomes readable shorthand for other developers. Another objective is to recognize misuse: patterns can be misapplied when they solve a one-off problem or add indirection with no clear benefit. Finally, you will complete a hands-on Observer exercise to reinforce how patterns structure interactions between objects. These skills are less about memorizing UML and more about making pragmatic decisions: start simple, spot repetition or frequent change, then introduce a pattern to manage that variability. Use the verification milestones to self-check whether your refactor actually simplifies tests, reduces conditionals, and makes the code easier to extend.

screens.title: What is a Design Pattern?
screens.subtitle: A reusable solution template for recurring design problems

narration.text: Start with a clear definition: a design pattern is a general, reusable solution to a commonly occurring problem in a particular context. It is not a finished implementation, but a template that identifies roles, responsibilities, and relationships so you can apply the structure in your code. The key benefit is reuse of design intent — when you declare a pattern, other developers instantly infer responsibilities and interaction models. A concrete example: the Strategy pattern separates the selection of an algorithm from the code that uses it. Instead of embedding conditional branches that check types or flags, you define an interface and multiple implementations, then inject the chosen strategy. A common misconception is that patterns are only for large systems. In fact, they help at any scale when you have repeated variability or frequent change points. The takeaway is practical: look for repetition or conditional complexity, then refactor toward a pattern that isolates the changing part. Ask yourself: does this part of the code change for different reasons than the rest? If yes, a pattern can help isolate those changes. What is a Design Pattern? means design patterns capture roles and interactions so you can reuse solutions and communicate intent across teams.. In practical terms, a reusable solution template for recurring design problems. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Design patterns capture roles and interactions so you can reuse solutions and communicate intent across teams.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › What is a Design Pattern?
Definition & Purpose
A design pattern is a reusable solution to a common problem within a context. It specifies roles, collaborations, and responsibilities so you can apply the same structure across different implementations without copying code.
Why it matters
Patterns improve readability and reduce ad-hoc complexity by making intent explicit.
Common misconception
Patterns are not mandatory for every feature. Use them where variability repeats or requirements change often.
Key Takeaway

Patterns encode intent and isolate change. Spot repetition or frequent variation first, then refactor toward a pattern.

Concrete example
Imagine payment processing with multiple gateways. Without a pattern, the checkout code checks types and performs gateway-specific steps. With a pattern like Strategy, each gateway is a separate class implementing a common interface, so the checkout code only calls the interface methods.
  • Definition: a template that describes object roles and interactions.
  • Example: Strategy isolates payment algorithms into their own classes.
  • When to use: when you see repeated conditional logic or changing algorithms.
Check your understanding
Identify one place in current code where responsibilities change for different reasons and describe which pattern might help isolate that change.

screens.title: Patterns and SOLID Principles
screens.subtitle: How patterns map to maintainability and extensibility

narration.text: Design patterns and SOLID principles are complementary. Patterns are structural choices that help you follow principles such as Single Responsibility and Open/Closed. For example, Strategy supports Open/Closed because you can add new algorithm implementations without changing the client. Factory Method supports Dependency Inversion by letting the client depend on an abstract creator instead of concrete product classes. Decorator helps Single Responsibility by keeping the core component focused and delegating add-on behavior to decorators. A practical way to evaluate a pattern is to ask: does introducing this pattern reduce the need to modify existing tested code when adding features? If yes, it often helps. A common misconception is that patterns replace reading SOLID; instead, they operationalize SOLID in code structure. Concrete scenario: if you find a class doing both data formatting and input and output, split responsibilities and consider a Decorator or separate formatter object. The takeaway: choose patterns that make a specific principle easier to uphold and verify with unit tests that changes are isolated. Patterns and SOLID Principles means use patterns to make solid principles easier to maintain in code and to reduce modification scope when requirements change.. In practical terms, how patterns map to maintainability and extensibility. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Design + Principle
keyIdea.text: Use patterns to make SOLID principles easier to maintain in code and to reduce modification scope when requirements change.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Patterns and SOLID Principles
Pattern → Principle mapping
Strategy
Enables Open/Closed and SRP by separating algorithms into interchangeable classes.
Factory Method
Promotes Dependency Inversion and loose coupling by deferring instantiation.
Decorator
Supports SRP by moving auxiliary behavior out of the core component.

Evaluate a pattern by checking whether adding a feature requires modifying existing tested classes. If introducing a pattern localizes change, it likely aids maintainability.

Key Takeaway

Pick patterns that make one SOLID principle easier to enforce in your code base; avoid adding patterns whose benefit is unclear.

Practical scenario
A report generator with many format-specific if-else blocks is a classic signal. Use Strategy to encapsulate formatting algorithms and Factory to create the appropriate formatter based on user selection. This reduces the need to change the generator when adding formats.
Common misuse
Applying a pattern to a feature that won't change or repeat often increases indirection without benefits. Prefer simple code first, then refactor when the pattern’s advantages become clear.

screens.title: Strategy Pattern — Structure and Example
screens.subtitle: Encapsulate algorithms and swap them at runtime (C# example)

narration.text: The Strategy pattern defines a family of algorithms and makes them interchangeable through a common interface. The client depends on the abstraction, not concrete implementations, so adding a new strategy requires only a new class that implements the interface. In the C# example you will see an IPaymentStrategy interface and separate classes for CreditCardPayment and PayPalPayment. The Order class acts as the context: it holds a reference to the strategy and delegates payment processing. A concrete example: when a user selects PayPal, the UI sets the PayPal strategy on the Order; the order then calls the strategy’s process method during checkout. A common misconception is that Strategy always requires runtime swapping — sometimes strategy selection happens once at construction time and remains fixed, which is still a valid use. The main testable benefit is that each strategy can be unit-tested in isolation, and the context’s logic remains small and focused. Consider whether the branching in your code represents algorithms that vary independently — if so, Strategy is a good fit. Strategy Pattern — Structure and Example means isolate algorithms behind an interface so you can add or test them independently without changing the client.. In practical terms, encapsulate algorithms and swap them at runtime (c# example). A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Strategy Benefit
keyIdea.text: Isolate algorithms behind an interface so you can add or test them independently without changing the client.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Strategy Pattern
C# Example (illustrative)
Interface and implementations isolate payment algorithms from Order logic.
// Strategy Pattern Example (C#)

// 1. Define the Strategy Interface
public interface IPaymentStrategy
{
  void ProcessPayment(decimal amount);
}

// 2. Implement Concrete Strategies
public class CreditCardPayment : IPaymentStrategy
{
  public void ProcessPayment(decimal amount)
  {
    Console.WriteLine($"Processing credit card payment for ${amount}");
  }
}

public class PayPalPayment : IPaymentStrategy
{
  public void ProcessPayment(decimal amount)
  {
    Console.WriteLine($"Processing PayPal payment for ${amount}");
  }
}

// 3. Context class that uses a Strategy
public class Order
{
  private IPaymentStrategy _paymentStrategy;
  private decimal _amount;

  public Order(decimal amount)
  {
    _amount = amount;
  }

  public void SetPaymentStrategy(IPaymentStrategy strategy)
  {
    _paymentStrategy = strategy;
  }

  public void Checkout()
  {
    if (_paymentStrategy == null)
    {
      Console.WriteLine("No payment strategy set. Cannot checkout.");
      return;
    }
    _paymentStrategy.ProcessPayment(_amount);
  }
}
  • Context holds a reference to the strategy interface.
  • Concrete strategies implement the algorithm and are independently testable.
  • Adding a new payment type requires a new class, not changing Order.
Key Takeaway

Strategy reduces conditional complexity by moving variable behavior into separate, testable classes.

Common mistakes
Turning every small variation into its own strategy can add unnecessary classes. Use Strategy when variations are substantial or change independently.
Pro tip
Prefer constructor injection when the strategy won’t change frequently; prefer setter injection when runtime switching is required.

screens.title: When to Use Strategy — A Practical Checklist
screens.subtitle: Decision steps to determine if Strategy fits your problem

narration.text: Before applying a pattern, run a quick checklist. First, identify whether there is repeated conditional logic or multiple algorithms performing the same role. Second, verify the algorithms change for reasons distinct from the client class—if so, they are likely to vary independently. Third, check whether encapsulating the algorithms into separate classes will simplify testing or reduce changes to the client. Fourth, estimate the lifecycle: if new algorithms are expected in the future, Strategy helps you add them without modifying existing code. A concrete scenario: a report generator that handles PDF and Excel formats with if-else blocks. If you anticipate adding a new format or having different teams own format behavior, replace conditionals with separate formatter strategies. A common misconception is thinking Strategy always requires runtime swapping; selecting a strategy once at construction is common and still yields the benefits of isolation and testability. The key takeaway is to prefer a small refactor toward an interface and one or two implementations, then expand as patterns prove useful. When to Use Strategy — A Practical Checklist means apply strategy when you have repeated conditional algorithms that vary independently and benefit from isolated testing and extension.. In practical terms, decision steps to determine if strategy fits your problem. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Checklist
keyIdea.text: Apply Strategy when you have repeated conditional algorithms that vary independently and benefit from isolated testing and extension.

screens.title: Factory Method — Structure and Java Example
screens.subtitle: Decouple creation from usage to support extensibility

narration.text: The Factory Method defines an interface for creating an object, letting subclasses decide which concrete class to instantiate. The benefit is loose coupling: client code depends on abstract products and creators rather than concrete classes. The Java example illustrates a Document interface and concrete products like WordDocument and PdfDocument. A DocumentCreator declares the factory method createDocument, and concrete creators implement it to return the right product. When the client calls manageDocument on the creator, the concrete subclass determines the actual product type. This defers decision-making to subclasses and isolates creation logic. A common misconception is that Factory Method is only about factories — instead, it’s about delegating the choice of concrete implementation to subclasses so the client remains unaware of concrete types. The practical advantage is clear when you add a new document type: create the product and a new creator subclass without changing existing client code. The key takeaway is that Factory Method centralizes and isolates instantiation, which reduces ripple effects when adding types. Factory Method — Structure and Java Example means centralize object creation to decouple clients from concrete classes and make the system easier to extend.. In practical terms, decouple creation from usage to support extensibility. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Factory Benefit
keyIdea.text: Centralize object creation to decouple clients from concrete classes and make the system easier to extend.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Factory Method
Java Example (illustrative)
Creator defers instantiation to subclasses so clients remain decoupled from concrete products.
// Factory Method Example (Java)

// 1. Product Interface
interface Document {
  void open();
  void save();
}

// 2. Concrete Products
class WordDocument implements Document {
  public void open() { System.out.println("Opening Word Document."); }
  public void save() { System.out.println("Saving Word Document."); }
}

class PdfDocument implements Document {
  public void open() { System.out.println("Opening PDF Document."); }
  public void save() { System.out.println("Saving PDF Document."); }
}

// 3. Creator Abstract Class with Factory Method
abstract class DocumentCreator {
  public abstract Document createDocument();

  public void manageDocument() {
    Document doc = createDocument();
    doc.open();
    doc.save();
  }
}

// 4. Concrete Creators
class WordDocumentCreator extends DocumentCreator {
  @Override
  public Document createDocument() { return new WordDocument(); }
}

class PdfDocumentCreator extends DocumentCreator {
  @Override
  public Document createDocument() { return new PdfDocument(); }
}
  • Creators expose a factory method; subclasses decide concrete product types.
  • Adding a product requires a new concrete product and creator, not changes to clients.
  • Factory Method supports DIP by keeping clients dependent on abstractions.
Key Takeaway

Factory Method isolates instantiation choices so new product types can be added with minimal changes.

When to choose Factory
Use Factory Method when a class can’t anticipate the exact concrete type it must create, or when subclasses should decide the product variants.
Common mistake
Using a complex factory hierarchy for a handful of product types increases indirection. Prefer simple factories or dependency injection when appropriate.

screens.title: Decorator Pattern — Extend Behavior Without Subclassing
screens.subtitle: Add responsibilities dynamically and chain decorators (Python example)

narration.text: The Decorator pattern adds responsibilities to an object dynamically without modifying the original class or creating many subclasses. It works by wrapping the original component in decorator objects that implement the same interface and delegate to the wrapped component while adding behavior. The Python example shows a SimpleCoffee component and decorators such as MilkDecorator and SugarDecorator that add cost and ingredients. A practical example: adding logging, caching, or formatting behaviors at runtime without affecting the base component. A common misconception is confusing Decorator with inheritance — Decorator composes behavior. Another trap is excessive decorator chains that make reasoning about final behavior harder; prefer clear ordering and name decorators to reflect their effect. The key value is flexibility: you can compose decorators in different orders to produce different combined behaviors without changing the core component class or creating combinatorial subclasses. Decorator Pattern — Extend Behavior Without Subclassing means compose behaviors around a core component to add features dynamically without subclass explosion.. In practical terms, add responsibilities dynamically and chain decorators (python example). A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Decorator Benefit
keyIdea.text: Compose behaviors around a core component to add features dynamically without subclass explosion.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Decorator Pattern
Python Example (illustrative)
Decorators wrap a component to add behavior while preserving the component interface.
# Decorator Pattern Example (Python)

class Coffee:
    def get_cost(self):
        return 5
    def get_ingredients(self):
        return "Coffee"

class SimpleCoffee(Coffee):
    def get_cost(self):
        return 5
    def get_ingredients(self):
        return "Simple Coffee"

class CoffeeDecorator(Coffee):
    def __init__(self, decorated_coffee):
        self._decorated_coffee = decorated_coffee

    def get_cost(self):
        return self._decorated_coffee.get_cost()

    def get_ingredients(self):
        return self._decorated_coffee.get_ingredients()

class MilkDecorator(CoffeeDecorator):
    def __init__(self, decorated_coffee):
        super().__init__(decorated_coffee)
        self._cost_milk = 1.5
        self._ingredient_milk = ", Milk"

    def get_cost(self):
        return super().get_cost() + self._cost_milk

    def get_ingredients(self):
        return super().get_ingredients() + self._ingredient_milk
  • Decorators preserve the component interface and delegate calls to the wrapped object.
  • Chaining decorators composes behavior; ordering can affect the result.
  • Use when you need dynamic, runtime combinations of behavior without subclassing.
Key Takeaway

Decorator provides flexible composition for features that can be combined differently at runtime, avoiding subclass explosion.

Common mistakes
Overusing decorators when a simple property or flag would suffice, or creating long, hard-to-trace decorator chains without clear naming and ordering rules.
Analogy
Think of the component as a plain cake and decorators as toppings you can add at will — mix and match without baking a new cake every time.

screens.title: Over-engineering and Misuse of Patterns
screens.subtitle: How to spot when a pattern harms clarity instead of helping it

narration.text: Patterns can be misused. Over-engineering happens when a pattern is applied to a problem that is not recurring, adding indirection and cognitive overhead rather than reducing it. Common signals include an explosion of small classes, many tiny interfaces, or a factory hierarchy for only one or two product types. A practical rule: prefer the simplest design that passes tests and then refactor when you see repetition or changing requirements. For instance, if you add Strategy for a single, unlikely-to-change algorithm, you probably increased complexity for no gain. Another misuse is premature generalization: designing a pattern interface around hypothetical future needs that never materialize. Always verify that the pattern reduces modification points in practice — if adding a new feature still touches many files, the chosen pattern might be the wrong one. The takeaway: introduce patterns incrementally, run tests, and ensure the refactor reduces maintenance effort. Ask: did the change reduce the number of places I must modify for a common change? Over-engineering and Misuse of Patterns means introduce patterns only when they reduce actual modification points and support recurring variability; otherwise prefer simplicity.. In practical terms, how to spot when a pattern harms clarity instead of helping it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Avoid Over-engineering
keyIdea.text: Introduce patterns only when they reduce actual modification points and support recurring variability; otherwise prefer simplicity.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Over-engineering
When patterns become harmful
Over-engineering stems from applying abstractions before a real need exists. This often creates more code to read and reason about without reducing maintenance effort.
Signal: many tiny classes
A large number of trivial classes often indicates over-abstraction.
Signal: speculative interfaces
Designing for hypothetical features that never arrive wastes effort.

Practical guideline: implement the simplest working solution, write tests, and only extract a pattern when repetition or change justifies the refactor. Use code reviews to ask whether a pattern actually reduces modification points.

Quick checklist
  1. Is the problem recurring?
  2. Does the pattern localize change?
  3. Does it simplify testing?
Key Takeaway

Prefer simplicity. Introduce patterns only to manage real, observed complexity and prove the benefits with tests.

screens.title: Implement the Observer Pattern — Activity
screens.subtitle: Notify multiple displays from a WeatherStation (starter code provided)

narration.text: This hands-on activity asks you to implement the Observer pattern in Python for a WeatherStation that notifies multiple displays. The goal is to practice turning a design intention into a concrete Subject and Observer interface. Start by creating an Observer interface with an update method that accepts temperature and humidity. Make CurrentConditionsDisplay and StatisticsDisplay implement that interface. Next, modify WeatherStation to act as the Subject: add register_observer and remove_observer methods and a notify_observers method that calls update on each registered observer. In set_measurements call notify_observers after updating internal state. A concrete benefit is decoupling the station from specific displays: you can add new displays without changing WeatherStation. A common mistake is exposing internal state directly; instead, pass only the minimal data needed to observers. After implementing, register displays in the main block and run the example to confirm displays receive updates. The key question: did your design allow adding a new display type without editing WeatherStation? Implement the Observer Pattern — Activity means practice creating a subject and observers so the weatherstation can notify displays without knowing their concrete types.. In practical terms, notify multiple displays from a weatherstation (starter code provided). A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Activity Goal
keyIdea.text: Practice creating a Subject and Observers so the WeatherStation can notify displays without knowing their concrete types.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Observer Activity
Starter Code (Python)
Add the Observer interface, register/remove methods, and notify logic in WeatherStation.
# observer_pattern_starter.py

class WeatherStation:
    def __init__(self):
        self._temperature = 0
        self._humidity = 0
        # How do we notify displays? This is where the pattern comes in.

    def set_measurements(self, temperature, humidity):
        self._temperature = temperature
        self._humidity = humidity
        print(f"WeatherStation: New measurements set: Temp={temperature}°C, Humidity={humidity}%")
        # TODO: Notify registered observers here

class CurrentConditionsDisplay:
    def update(self, temperature, humidity):
        print(f"CurrentConditionsDisplay: Temperature={temperature}°C, Humidity={humidity}%")

class StatisticsDisplay:
    def update(self, temperature, humidity):
        # In a real app, calculate min/max/avg
        print(f"StatisticsDisplay: Avg Temp={temperature}°C, Max Humidity={humidity}% (simplified)")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    station = WeatherStation()
    current_display = CurrentConditionsDisplay()
    stats_display = StatisticsDisplay()

    # How to register and notify?
    station.set_measurements(25, 65)
    station.set_measurements(27, 70)
Implementation steps
  1. Create an Observer interface with update(temperature, humidity).
  2. Make displays implement Observer and its update method.
  3. Add register_observer, remove_observer, and notify_observers to WeatherStation.
  4. Call notify_observers from set_measurements after updating state.
Hints & pitfalls
Keep WeatherStation unaware of concrete display types. Pass only the data observers need rather than exposing internals.
Reflection
After implementing, add a new display and register it. If WeatherStation requires no changes, your pattern application succeeded.
Key Takeaway

Observer decouples subject and observers so changes to display logic don’t ripple through the data source.

screens.title: Three Common Mistakes for Each Pattern
screens.subtitle: Avoiding unnecessary complexity and preserving clarity

narration.text: Let’s summarize frequent mistakes when applying the three patterns. For Strategy, developers often create strategies for trivial differences, which increases class count without value. A better approach is to refactor only when algorithms differ in meaningful ways or when tests benefit. For Factory Method, a common error is building deep factory hierarchies for a small number of product types; in such cases prefer simple factories or dependency injection. For Decorator, the mistake is over-chaining anonymous decorators and losing track of runtime behavior ordering. Always give decorators clear names and document expected composition order. A second class of mistakes is failing to test isolated units: each strategy or decorator should have focused tests. Finally, misuse often stems from skipping the diagnostic question: does this pattern reduce the number of places I must change for a given feature? If not, reconsider. The closing takeaway: patterns are tools to reduce maintenance cost; use them only where they demonstrably reduce modification scope and improve testability. Three Common Mistakes for Each Pattern means apply patterns only when they localize change, simplify testing, and reduce modification points; avoid premature abstraction.. keyIdea.text: Apply patterns only when they localize change, simplify testing, and reduce modification points; avoid premature abstraction.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Common Mistakes
Patterns — common pitfalls
Strategy
Don’t create a strategy for trivial flags. Refactor when algorithms truly vary or tests benefit.
Factory Method
Avoid deep factory hierarchies when only a couple of product types exist; use simpler creation patterns instead.
Decorator
Naming and composition order matter; long anonymous chains can be hard to debug.

Testing note: unit tests should target each isolated strategy, factory, or decorator. If tests still require heavy setup or touching many files, the chosen pattern may not be simplifying the design.

Quick remedy
Introduce patterns incrementally. Add tests and measure whether the refactor reduces modification scope and simplifies reasoning.
Key Takeaway

Patterns should simplify maintenance. Use tests and small refactors to confirm that they do.

screens.title: Putting It Together — Small Refactor Workflow
screens.subtitle: A step-by-step approach to introduce a pattern safely

narration.text: A safe workflow reduces risk when introducing patterns. Step one: identify a recurring problem or a class with multiple responsibilities. Step two: write a failing test or a regression test that captures the current behaviour you must preserve. Step three: perform a minimal refactor — extract an interface or a small class to isolate the varying part. Step four: add one concrete pattern implementation and run tests. Step five: expand only if repetition or new requirements justify more structure. A concrete walkthrough: convert a report generator’s conditional branches into separate formatter classes. Start by extracting an IFormatter interface and a minimal unit test for the generator using a mock formatter. After tests pass, implement a Factory or Strategy to create or select formatters. This incremental approach preserves behavior, keeps commits small, and gives quick feedback. A common mistake is refactoring large portions at once; prefer focused steps and tests that verify each small change. The result is a cleaner codebase with measured, reversible improvements. Step-by-step process
1
Identify the real pain
Find repeated conditionals or a class with multiple reasons to change.
2
Write a test that captures behavior
Create a focused test so refactors are safe and reversible.
3
Extract a minimal abstraction
Introduce an interface or small class that isolates the varying part.
4
Implement the pattern incrementally
Add one strategy, factory, or decorator and keep tests green.
This incremental approach keeps commits small, preserves behavior, and provides fast feedback. If the pattern doesn’t simplify tests or reduce modification points, roll back and try a simpler refactor.
Concrete example
Extract an IFormatter, create a mock formatter for tests, then implement PdfFormatter and ExcelFormatter as separate classes. Use a Factory to create the right formatter from a setting.
Key Takeaway

Small, test-backed refactors are the safest path to applying patterns and improving maintainability.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Remember these concise concepts as you apply patterns. A Design Pattern is a reusable solution template for common design problems, intended to communicate intent and structure. The Strategy Pattern encapsulates algorithms so they can vary independently from clients, reducing conditional complexity. The Factory Method delegates object creation to subclasses to decouple clients from concrete types and support extensibility. These three concepts are foundational: use them to make code easier to extend and to reduce the number of places you must change for a feature. Before applying a pattern, ask whether it will reduce modification points and simplify testing; prefer simple refactors first. Practice the hands-on Observer task to solidify how patterns decouple components. Carry these ideas into code reviews: identify repetition, prefer interfaces where appropriate, and avoid premature abstraction. Which concept will you apply next time you see repeated conditionals in your code?

keyIdea.text: Use patterns that isolate change and communicate intent — Strategy for algorithms, Factory for creation, Decorator for composition.

Key Concepts
Design Pattern
A reusable solution template to a common design problem.
Strategy Pattern
Encapsulates interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface.
Factory Method
Defers object creation to subclasses to reduce coupling.
Decorator
Adds behavior dynamically by wrapping components.
Over-engineering
Applying patterns where they do not reduce modification or complexity.
SOLID Principles
Patterns help operationalize principles like SRP, OCP, and DIP.
Summary
Use patterns to localize change and express design intent. Start simple, add patterns incrementally, and validate benefits with tests.

narration.text: Finish with an action checklist. First, when you see repeated conditional logic, consider Strategy to encapsulate algorithms. Second, when object creation couples clients to concrete types, consider Factory Method to centralize instantiation. Third, when you need dynamic feature composition, use Decorator to wrap and extend behavior without subclassing. Always validate pattern adoption with tests and small refactors. Avoid patterns that increase the number of places you must change for a given requirement. The most practical insight is that patterns are communication tools: they make your design readable to others. As a closing question, pick one repeating code smell in your project and plan a minimal, test-backed refactor that applies one of these patterns.
